docs.text: Architecture Overview The central file of Dotboost is .claude/settings.json . It registers the hooks, sets the permission tiers, and configures the status line. It does not set personal preferences (permission mode, theme, TUI, spinner verbs). Each developer sets them in their own settings.local.json , and settings.local.json.example contains a sample. Outside this file, the payload has no wiring. Claude Code finds skills and commands from their directory location only. The four artifact types Type Where it lives How it activates Hook .claude/hooks/*.sh settings.json registers it for a lifecycle event ( SessionStart , PreToolUse , PostToolUse ). It always runs when its event and matcher fire. Skill .claude/skills/*/SKILL.md Claude Code loads it automatically when its description: frontmatter matches the current task of the conversation. There is no routing table. Command .claude/commands/*.md You start it explicitly by name, for example /dk-review . Subagent .claude/agents/*.md A command starts it, or Claude starts it by its own decision. For example, the review flow delegates to dotkernel-reviewer . This is important because the four types fail in different ways. When settings.json does not register a hook, the hook never runs. A skill can be present but have a vague description: , and then Claude may never select it. This is not an error: nothing happens, and you see no message. A command only exists when you type its name. To debug "why didn't Dotboost do X", first identify which of these four categories X belongs to. Two layers of guardrail Dotboost protects the target repository at two independent layers: Permission tiers ( permissions.deny / ask / allow in settings.json ): path-glob rules and command-prefix rules that Claude Code enforces natively. Hooks ( guard-protected-paths.sh , guard-bash.sh ): bash scripts that examine the actual tool call. They also examine compound Bash commands ( cd src && composer require foo ), and a glob pattern cannot see inside these commands. The two layers overlap intentionally, but they do not agree on all commands. A hook blocks some commands that the tier list marks as ask . For the specific list, see Guardrails vs. Permissions . This difference is the most frequent cause of the confusion "why did it refuse instead of prompting me". The CLAUDE.md contract Three behaviors need a short block in the CLAUDE.md of the consuming project: the dependency policy in dotkernel-package-status the feature-docs check the ASD-STE100 writing style in dotkernel-writing-style Until the project pastes the block into its own CLAUDE.md , these behaviors are only loadable. After that, they become proactive . The description: frontmatter of a skill decides whether the skill can load. It does not decide whether Claude uses the skill when nobody asks for it. Thus, when you install only .claude/ , these three behaviors do not operate fully. For more information, see Getting Started and Feature Documentation . What's next Permissions for the guardrail tiers. Hooks for the six lifecycle scripts. Skills for how the nineteen skills are organized.

docs.text: Feature Documentation /dk-document writes one markdown file for each feature into the target project. The file tells what the feature does and why, the routes and roles that reach it, the data it adds, and how to try it. A cleared session cannot find this part of a change again from src/ alone. For this reason, it is a file in the repo and not a note in a chat transcript. Where it lands The skill finds the location in the repo and does not guess it. Many Dotkernel repositories already have a documentation/ directory, with command docs, a generated openapi.json and Postman collections. The standard API has this directory, but derived projects are different. Thus the skill checks the repo and does not infer: documentation/features/ when the repo already has a documentation/ directory docs/features/ otherwise It never creates a second documentation root next to an existing one. Both paths are in the allow permission tier. Prose in a docs directory is approximately the write with the lowest risk in the tree. The review uses the frontmatter The frontmatter of each feature doc has routes: and handlers: . /dk-review greps these keys to find whether a doc describes each new route in the current diff. It reports a doc that is missing or out of date as Should fix . /dk-review never writes a doc itself. It is read-only by design, and it tells you to run /dk-document . Make Claude read the docs before a change Claude writes a doc only when you ask for it. You can make Claude look for an existing doc before it adds or changes behaviour in that area. To do this, add this block to the CLAUDE.md of the project: ## Feature docs Before you add or change behaviour, examine `docs/features/` (or `documentation/features/`) for a doc about that area. If a doc exists, read it. After the change, update that doc, or write a new doc with `/dk-document`. A doc that does not agree with the code is a bug in the doc. The session-start hook always prints the directory and the number of docs. Thus Claude can find the files without this block. But the block makes Claude actually read them.

docs.text: Getting Started Install Select one way. Both ways install the same files. Clone it inside the project cd <project> git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/dotkernel/dotboost.git .dotboost mkdir -p .claude cp -r .dotboost/.claude/. .claude/ rm -rf .dotboost Download the zip This way does not need git: cd <project> curl -L -o dotboost.zip https://github.com/dotkernel/dotboost/archive/refs/heads/main.zip unzip -q dotboost.zip mkdir -p .claude cp -r dotboost-main/.claude/. .claude/ rm -rf dotboost-main dotboost.zip After copying, either way chmod +x .claude/hooks/*.sh .claude/statusline.sh echo '.claude/settings.local.json' >> .git/info/exclude The payload commits no file with an executable bit. Also, a zip that you extract on Windows has no permission bits at all. settings.json runs the hooks and the status line as bash <path> , so they run without the bits. The chmod is necessary only when you run one of them manually. The settings.local.json line keeps personal, git-ignored overrides out of git add . . The trailing /. copies the contents of the .claude/ directory in the payload. Thus, the copy merges into an existing .claude/ directory. It does not put a second directory at .claude/.claude/ . But the merge still overwrites the files that have the same name. If the target project already has its own .claude/settings.json or .claude/commands/ , merge the files manually. Do not run the copy without a check. Add the CLAUDE.md block Three behaviors need a short block in the project's own CLAUDE.md : the dependency policy in dotkernel-package-status the feature-docs check the writing style in dotkernel-writing-style Without the block, these behaviors are only loadable. With the block, they become proactive. For more information, see Architecture Overview and Package Status . All Dotkernel projects and packages write prose in ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English. Paste this block to make the dotkernel-writing-style skill always active: ## Writing style Write all prose in ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English. This includes chat answers, commit and tag messages, MR/PR descriptions, Markdown files, code comments, docblock descriptions, exception messages, CLI output and OpenAPI descriptions. Do not apply it to the code itself: identifiers, keywords, syntax and docblock tags stay as they are. Load the `dotkernel-writing-style` skill before you write any of this prose. Optional: markdown linting .claude/hooks/markdown-lint.sh checks each .md file that Claude writes against .claude/markdownlint.jsonc . It needs markdownlint-cli2 , which Dotboost does not include: npm install -g markdownlint-cli2 A project-local devDependency also works. The hook uses ./node_modules/.bin/markdownlint-cli2 first, and uses the global one when the local one is not available. Until the hook can find the binary, it exits without output. Thus, .claude/ stays drop-in for projects that have no Node toolchain. Verify Start Claude Code in the project, and run /help . You should see dk-bootstrap , dk-module , dk-route , dk-trace , dk-test , dk-document , dk-check , dk-deprecate , dk-review , dk-hygiene . The session-start hook should start with a short briefing. The briefing shows the detected project variant, the root namespace and the authorization style. It flags a guard policy that leaves unlisted routes public. It also shows which config files are still missing. Verifying an Install gives the full end-to-end verification steps. It also tells how to test the guardrails themselves.

You start it explicitly by its name, which is different from a skill. dot-maker dotkernel/dot-maker , a Composer tool ( composer make … ). docs.text: Introduction Dotboost is a drop-in Claude Code configuration for Dotkernel projects. It is not a Dotkernel project, not a library, and not a package for composer require . This repository contains no composer.json and no PHP source at all. Its full payload is a .claude/ directory: settings, hooks, a status line, a review subagent, ten /dk-* slash commands and nineteen skills. To install it, copy that directory into the root of the Dotkernel project that you actually work on. This can be an API, Admin, Frontend, Light or Queue project, or a project derived from one of them. The problem it solves Claude Code has no built-in knowledge of the Dotkernel conventions, for example: how to name a handler where an entity belongs (an application module or the shared Core submodule) which PSR applies where how authorization keys map to routes the difference between a HAL-based API response and a templated redirect Without that knowledge, an agent in a Dotkernel repository asks too many questions. Or it writes code with confidence, and that code does not match the house style. Dotboost solves this problem in two ways: Skills teach the conventions: naming, structure, validation, responses, security, testing and PSR standards. Claude Code loads each skill automatically when its description matches your task. Hooks and permissions protect the repository while an agent works in it: They block edits to vendor/ , dependency manifests, migrations and secrets. They block shell commands that are destructive or that install dependencies. They normalize whitespace and line endings in each file that Claude changes. Who this is for Dotboost is for each person who uses Claude Code in a Dotkernel repository. This includes developers on a Dotkernel project, and maintainers of a project derived from one of the Dotkernel starter kits. It is equally useful when you build a new feature, review a PR or bootstrap a fresh clone. What's next Architecture Overview explains how the parts work together. Getting Started tells how to install Dotboost into a project.

docs.text: Status Line .claude/statusline.sh shows the real account and session usage in the status bar. It reads the data from the JSON payload that Claude Code (≥ 2.1) sends to the status line on stdin. The rate limits are the same numbers that /usage reports: ~/project Opus 5.5 · high $ 0.45 ctx ▰▱▱▱▱▱ 6% 5h ███████▍ 37% ↻ 2h 14m (16:20) 7d ▰▰▰▰▰▰▱▱▱▱ 61% The first line is a row of coloured chips, then the context gauge: the working directory, the model and its effort level. $ : the estimated billed cost of the session. It stays at 0.00 while both rate limits are less than 100%. When one of them reaches 100%, and for all the time that the model is Fable, it adds the increase of the USD estimate from Claude Code ( cost.total_cost_usd ). The payload has no field for billed credit, so this value is an estimate at API prices, not an invoice. The script keeps the running total for each session in ${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/claude-statusline-<session_id>.cost . It assigns each increase to the state that is true when the status line redraws. ctx : how full the context window is ( context_window.used_percentage ). The second line has the gauges for the rate limits. The 5-hour window shows as a heat gradient of 20 cells with its reset time, then the 7-day window shows. If the payload does not have a field, the status line does not show it (for example, the rate limits with an API key). The colours are 24-bit, so the terminal must support truecolor. The script uses only bash and awk . It does not use jq or Python, it does not scan transcripts, and it does not guess token budgets. Thus it also works in Git Bash on Windows. docs.text: .claude/statusline.sh shows the real account and session usage in the status bar. It reads the data from the JSON payload that Claude Code (≥ 2.1) sends to the status line on stdin. docs.text: Windows and Line Endings Dotkernel repos have a .gitattributes file with * text eol=lf , which controls all files that git checks out. For more safety, also configure the client, so that no conversion occurs in either direction: git config core.autocrlf false git config core.eol lf git config core.safecrlf warn Verify git config --get core.autocrlf # false git ls-files --eol | grep -v 'w/lf' | head # nothing for text files If CRLF is already committed, renormalize one time with git add --renormalize . . PhpStorm Set Editor → Code Style → Line separator = Unix (\n) . Set File Encodings → UTF-8 and Create UTF-8 files: with NO BOM . How Dotboost enforces this while working normalize-file.sh fixes BOM, CRLF, trailing whitespace, and the final newline in each file that Claude writes. See Hooks Reference . session-start.sh also gives a warning at the start of a session if it finds CRLF in the working tree. /dk-hygiene runs the same checks on a full set of changed files when you ask for it.

docs.text: Introduction A command is a .md file under .claude/commands/ with YAML frontmatter. The frontmatter has a description , an optional argument-hint , and allowed-tools , which limits the tools that the command can use. A command is different from a skill: it never loads automatically. You start it explicitly when you type its name, for example /dk-review . Dotboost has ten commands. They cover the lifecycle of a change, from a new clone to a diff that is ready for a PR. See Reference for the full list, in groups for each stage of the workflow. Commands vs. skills Use a command when you want a specific procedure that you can run again on request. Examples are to bootstrap a clone, to run the QA gate, or to write a feature doc. Use a skill when you want Claude to know something automatically while it works on other tasks. Examples are a naming convention, a validation pattern, or a security rule. Some commands use skills internally. For example, /dk-module uses dotkernel-dot-maker and dotkernel-module-structure , and does not copy their guidance. When the repo is an API project, /dk-route and /dk-review also load dotkernel-api-endpoint . Thus Claude builds and reviews a new endpoint against the same checklist.

docs.text: Guardrails vs. Permissions guard-bash.sh refuses some commands that the permission tiers in settings.json only mark ask . This is on purpose. The hook can see into compound Bash commands, and a path or prefix permission rule cannot. But because of this, you do not get the approval prompt that the ask tier gives. You get a refusal. Command settings.json says guard-bash.sh does git rebase ask blocks doctrine-migrations migrate / execute ask blocks fixtures:execute , schema:drop , schema:update (through bin/doctrine ) ask blocks git checkout -- ask, through git checkout blocks composer development-enable / -disable — blocks pip install , git filter-branch — blocks All the other items in the ask tier show a prompt, as Permissions Reference describes. These items include commits, mysql , and the config and QA files. Allow one of these commands again A change in settings.local.json does not remove a block at the hook level. That override layer changes only the permission tiers. To allow one of these commands, edit guard-bash.sh . Make this change on purpose, after you think about it. Each command in this table does one of these operations: It changes the database. It writes the git history again. It discards work that is not committed ( git checkout -- ). It installs packages ( pip install ). It changes the committed config state ( development-enable / -disable ). For this reason, the hook layer blocks it. A prompt is not sufficient, because a person can approve a prompt without attention.

docs.text: Introduction A hook is a bash script that settings.json registers for a Claude Code lifecycle event. Dotboost uses three events: SessionStart : runs when a session starts or resumes, and again after /clear or compaction. PreToolUse : runs before a tool call that matches Edit / Write / MultiEdit / NotebookEdit or Bash . It can block the call. PostToolUse : runs after a tool call that matches Edit / Write / MultiEdit . It cannot undo the call. It can only report on the result or normalize the result. Report-only vs. blocking The two PreToolUse hooks ( guard-protected-paths.sh , guard-bash.sh ) are guards. They refuse the call. The PostToolUse hooks are different. normalize-file.sh fixes whitespace and does not show a message. php-lint.sh and markdown-lint.sh are report-only on purpose. They do not run phpcbf or markdownlint --fix . When a hook formats a file immediately after Claude writes it, Claude's copy of the file in memory becomes incorrect. Then the next targeted edit in the same turn can fail. Do the bulk formatting at the end of a task, with composer cs-fix or /dk-check . Reference gives the full behavior of each hook. In some cases, a hook blocks a command that the permission tiers only mark ask . For these cases, see Guardrails vs. Permissions . Failure mode: consecutive edits to one file You can see "string not found" errors on consecutive edits to the same file. The usual cause is normalize-file.sh . It writes the file again between edits, and Claude's copy in memory becomes incorrect. Move the hook from PostToolUse to the Stop event. Then it runs one time for each turn, not one time for each edit.

docs.text: Reference Hook Event What it does guard-protected-paths.sh PreToolUse (Edit/Write) Blocks writes to vendor/ , node_modules/ , migrations, data/cache\|lock\|oauth/ , log/ , public/uploads/ , dependency manifests, tool caches, .git/ internals, and binary or key material ( *.png , *.zip , *.phar , *.key , *.pem ). Claude can edit the template, and the user applies it guard-bash.sh PreToolUse (Bash) Blocks installs, destructive git commands, commands that change the database, and development-mode toggles. It also blocks them inside a compound command, which permission globs cannot see into. Quoted arguments, comments and heredoc bodies are data, so grep "rm -rf" docs/ runs. docs.text: Customization The ask and allow tiers in Reference are personal preferences, not fixed policy. Override them for each machine in .claude/settings.local.json . This file is a layer on top of settings.json , and git ignores it. Never edit the shared file to make a rule less strict for yourself. cp .claude/settings.local.json.example .claude/settings.local.json Do not make the deny tier (never read, never written, never run) less strict in this way. It protects secrets and prevents destructive operations, for each person who runs the session. Session preferences The shared settings.json sets no permission mode, theme, UI or spinner verbs. settings.local.json.example has a sample of each. The samples are permissions.defaultMode: "auto" , theme: "dark" , tui: "fullscreen" and a spinnerVerbs list with a Dotkernel theme. Keep the samples that you want and delete the others. The defaultMode: "auto" entry only shows the key. It does not work from that file. Claude Code does not apply auto from project or local settings. The session starts without auto mode, and you get no error. To use auto mode, set permissions.defaultMode in ~/.claude/settings.json . See Permission modes . Status line placement settings.local.json.example also has a different statusLine.command . It points to ~/.claude/statusline.sh , not to the copy in the project. Use it if you want one shared status line for all projects, not one for each repo. See Status Line .

Claude's file tools and the Bash file commands that Claude Code recognises ( cat , head , tail , sed , tee ) cannot open these files. Never written : Edit denies, which also apply to Write . Claude does not silently run destructive git or install commands. They are rules, not a sandbox. They do not cover a command that reads files without their names ( grep -r password config/ ), or a script that opens a file itself. For a guarantee at the OS level, use the sandbox in the Claude Code permissions docs . Reference gives the full lists. This is intentionally less flexible than a skill. A prompt with a sufficiently strong argument can make Claude ignore a skill. It cannot make Claude ignore a deny rule in settings.json . docs.text: Package Status dotkernel-package-status controls each package decision in a Dotkernel project. It also tells whether a Dotkernel package is still maintained. It contains the dependency policy and the lookup in the package listing that dotkernel.com publishes. For this reason, it has its own page and not a row in Reference . The ladder Stop at the first hit: already in composer.lock dotkernel/* laminas/* / mezzio/* a vetted symfony / doctrine / psr / league package hand-rolled code The skill enforces this rule: never name a package from memory. A name is verified only when it is in composer.lock or in the dotkernel.com listing (below). The skill reports each other name as unverified. The source of truth is dotkernel.com Dotkernel publishes the support status of its open-source packages at https://www.dotkernel.com/dotkernel-packages.json . Dotkernel builds this file again each day from the GitHub organization. A version for human readers is at https://www.dotkernel.com/dotkernel-packages-oss-lifecycle/ . Each entry gives the lifecycle of the package ( active , maintenance , security-only or archived ), its php constraint, and the archived flag from GitHub. The skill fetches a new copy of the listing for each question. The skill does not generate, ship or store a file in the project, so you have nothing to refresh or git-ignore. The fetch needs network access. The fetch is not in the allow list or the deny list of settings.json , so it shows a prompt the first time. If the fetch fails, the skill calls dotkernel/* names that are not in composer.lock unverified. It does not use its memory as a fallback. No part of the skill queries Packagist. The skill reports a laminas/* , mezzio/* or community package that is not already installed as unverified. You must then confirm its maintenance status, its PHP support and its license. A general rule: an "actively maintained" package has a release in the last 12 months. It needs a CLAUDE.md block to be proactive The description: frontmatter of a skill only makes the skill loadable . It does not make Claude stop and think before Claude names a package that nobody asked for. That behavior must always be loaded. Thus it goes in the CLAUDE.md of the project that uses Dotboost , not in Dotboost: ## Dependency policy Use this order of preference, and stop at the first match: **already in composer.lock** -> **`dotkernel/*`** -> **`laminas/*` / `mezzio/*`** -> vetted `symfony|doctrine|psr|league` package -> hand-rolled code. - Never name a package from memory. Verify it against `composer.lock`, or against the `dotkernel/*` listing published at <https://www.dotkernel.com/dotkernel-packages.json>. Say that any other name is unverified. - Never run `composer require` in an upstream Dotkernel repository. Present a proposal. The user decides. - Before you suggest a package, use the `dotkernel-package-status` skill. This also applies to implicit suggestions: "how do I send mail from here?" is a package question. If the target project does not have this block, the skill can still load on an explicit package question. But a question with no package name in it ( "how do I send mail from here?" ) is much less likely to load the skill. When the listing is wrong Report a wrong or out-of-date entry in dotkernel/dotkernel.com . Report a wrong lifecycle value in the repository of the package, because its OSSMETADATA file declares the value. See Maintaining This .

docs.text: Introduction A skill is a directory under .claude/skills/ that contains a SKILL.md file. The file has frontmatter ( name , description ) and a body with instructions. There is no central routing table. Claude Code loads a skill automatically when its description: matches the work in the current conversation. Thus the description is the only activation mechanism. A skill with a vague or narrow description never loads, and you get no message and no error to debug. Dotboost has nineteen skills, all dotkernel-* . Each skill covers one part of the Dotkernel conventions. One of them, dotkernel-package-status , controls each package decision. It has sufficient detail for its own page . Each skill gives its scope in an Applies to block under its title. The block names the Dotkernel projects (API, Admin, Frontend, Light, Queue) and the packages that the skill covers. For example, dotkernel-api-endpoint applies only in an API project. There, it is the end-to-end checklist for a new or changed endpoint, and it points to the skill for each topic. Reading a trigger description The description of each skill includes the words that a developer actually types, for example "where does this go", "403" or "InputFilter". It does not include only the framework term for the concept. If a skill does not load when you expect it, the fix is almost always to add your phrase to its description. The fix is almost never to write its instructions again. See Maintaining This . Full list Reference puts all nineteen skills in groups by theme, with a one-line trigger description for each skill.
